10.25258/ijddt.16.88s.44.title: A Critical Review of Waste Biomass-Derived Carbon Dots for Drug Delivery: Synthesis, Properties, Applications, and Future Prospects
10.25258/ijddt.16.88s.44.abstract: Carbon dots (CDs) made from waste materials and renewable biomass are gaining popularity due to the growing need for sustainable and multipurpose medicine delivery systems. A promising strategy that addresses waste valorization and the creation of functional nanomaterials for therapeutic administration at the same time is waste-biomass-derived carbon dots (WBCDs). The synthesis, physicochemical characteristics, drug-delivery uses, biocompatibility, and translational potential of WBCDs are all rigorously examined in this review. The chemical composition of various waste biomass precursors— such as food wastes, plant-derived materials, agricultural residues, and chitin-rich wastes—and how it affects CD size, morphology, surface functionality, heteroatom incorporation, optical characteristics, and biological performance are examined. The main synthesis techniques—hydrothermal, microwave-assisted, microwave-hydrothermal, pyrolytic, ultrasonic, chemical oxidation, electrochemical, and conventional thermal approaches—are compared with a focus on how they affect characteristics important to drug delivery. Drug-loading processes, pH-responsive and controlled release, cellular uptake, targeted delivery, tracking using fluorescence, and theranostic uses are all given special consideration. The potential of WBCDs for delivering antibiotics, anticancer medications, anti-inflammatory medicines, and bioactive compounds is demonstrated by representative systems based on wheat bran, bamboo leaves, crab shells, sugarcane bagasse, sago bark, carrot roots, sea-buckthorn leaves, and other biomass sources. The review also emphasizes how precursor composition, surface chemistry, particle properties, purification, dose, and exposure conditions all have a significant impact on claimed biological safety. Biomass heterogeneity, batch-to-batch variability, purification, repeatability, limited control over drug loading and release, long-term toxicity, biodistribution, scalability, and regulatory translation are among the outstanding issues despite encouraging laboratory and preclinical results. Standardized synthesis, sophisticated characterisation, logical surface engineering, stimuli-responsive and target-specific administration, thorough toxicological evaluation, scalable processing, and life-cycle assessment should thus be the main areas of future development. All things considered, WBCDs are an emerging platform that combines multifunctional medication delivery technologies with the concepts of the circular economy.

10.25258/ijddt.16.88s.101.title: Phytochemical Profiling, In-Vitro COX-2 Inhibition and In-Silico Evaluation of the Ethanolic Flower Extract of Rosa indica L.
10.25258/ijddt.16.88s.101.abstract: Background: Pain and inflammation are leading reasons for medical care, and the adverse effects of long-term NSAID and opioid use sustain interest in safer plant-derived alternatives. Rosa indica L. (Rosaceae) is traditionally used for wounds, headaches, and inflammatory complaints, but its anti-inflammatory mechanism remains poorly defined. Objective: To chemically characterise the ethanolic flower extract of Rosa indica and evaluate its COX-2 inhibitory potential using integrated in vitro and in silico approaches. Methods: Fresh authenticated flowers were cold-macerated in 95 % ethanol and concentrated below 40°C. The extract underwent qualitative phytochemical screening, GC–MS profiling and a concentration-dependent COX-2 inhibition assay with indomethacin as a standard. Major constituents were docked against COX-2 (PDB: 5IKR), assessed for drug-likeness, and the resulting complexes were subjected to RMSF analysis using CABS-flex 3.0. Results: Screening confirmed phenolics, flavonoids, alkaloids, tannins, saponins, steroids and glycosides. GC–MS identified 27 constituents, including pyrogallol, 2,4-di-tert-butylphenol, 5-hydroxymethylfurfural, DDMP, phenylethyl alcohol, vanillin lactoside, linoleic acid, and chondroitin sulfate. Ethanolic extract of Rosa indica inhibited COX-2 with an IC₅₀ of 624.5 ± 23.33 µg/mL, compared with 93.35 ± 0.88 % inhibition by indomethacin. We describe a 77-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) whose only prominent symptoms were acute breathlessness with orthopnoea and a dull right hypochondrial ache; he remained afebrile throughout. 10.1108/jeim-05-2026-0911.title: Corporate ethical and responsible AI (CERAi) and AI trustworthiness: a lifecycle perspective and empirical insights
10.1108/jeim-05-2026-0911.abstract: Purpose This study develops and empirically validates a Corporate Ethical and Responsible AI (CERAi) lifecycle framework. The framework comprises three interdependent stages: design and development, testing and training, and deployment and usage. The study aims to move the research beyond abstract principles and policy analyses toward empirically grounded, lifecycle-integrated artificial intelligence AI governance theory. It positions ethical AI and responsible AI governance as the two constitutive components of the CERAi construct, and AI trustworthiness as a conceptually and empirically distinct downstream outcome anchored in stage-specific organizational governance mechanisms. The CERAi framework is scoped broadly to encompass governance of both conventional/traditional machine learning models and autonomous AI agents operating within organizational settings. Design/methodology/approach We administered a large-scale survey to 500 attendees at a national AI conference in the United States in early 2026, yielding 143 useable responses from AI professionals across healthcare, financial services, manufacturing, retail and energy sectors. We developed and validated multi-item scales for each CERAi lifecycle stage using established ethical AI and AI governance frameworks. Structural equation modeling was employed to assess the measurement model and to test both direct path hypotheses and mediation hypotheses. Findings Both CERAIi design and development and CERAi deployment and usage have significant positive direct effects on AI trustworthiness, whereas CERAi testing and training do not. Our results also indicate a significant serial mediation pathway in which CERAi deployment and usage enhance AI trustworthiness through testing and training, followed by design and development. Conversely, testing and training alone do not mediate the relationship between deployment and usage and AI trustworthiness, indicating that design-stage ethics serve as an intervening (mediating) mechanism through which governance activity enacted at later lifecycle stages is associated with perceived AI trustworthiness. This is consistent with testing and training's association with trustworthiness operating indirectly, mediated by the ethical architecture established during the design and development stage. Originality/value Findings of this study demonstrate that AI trustworthiness reflects differentiated perceived salience across AI lifecycle stages, whereby stakeholders appear to weight visible, deployment-stage governance more heavily than upstream design and testing stage governance in forming trustworthiness judgments, rather than reflecting a definitive validation that governance effects accumulate uniformly across all stages in isolation. This study makes a distinctive contribution by providing empirical evidence for a governance-sequencing mechanism, whereby design-stage ethics function as a mediating pathway shaping the effectiveness of governance activity at later lifecycle stages. To the best of our knowledge, such a mediated, stage-sequential mechanism has not previously been demonstrated using primary data within a comprehensive, three-stage CERAi lifecycle framework linking organizational ethical and responsible governance practices to AI trustworthiness outcomes.

10.1038/s42003-026-11125-8.title: Flippability of Escherichia coli membrane proteins under lipid stress reveals a new job for old genes
10.1038/s42003-026-11125-8.abstract: Normally, the “flip-flop” motion is reserved for small lipid molecules which move from one leaflet of the membrane to the other, and even that process is very slow without the aid of specific enzymes. Unexpectedly, we recently found that despite a prohibitively high energy barrier, Escherichia coli cardiolipin (CL) synthase A (ClsA) flips its large catalytic domain across the inner (cytoplasmic) membrane (IM) when cells were fully or partially depleted of phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and that this was necessary to support cell viability. Here, we demonstrated that production of the non-native phospholipid phosphatidylcholine (PC) in PE-depleted cells prevents ClsA flipping and halts cell growth, a phenotype rescued by constitutively inverted ClsA. Surprisingly, properly oriented lactose permease (LacY) acts as a multicopy suppressor, rescuing the growth defect in the -PE+PC cells. These data indicate that neutral PC regulates the membrane topology of ClsA and LacY, and subsequently the appearance of CL to the periplasmic leaflet required for viability. Therefore, ClsA and potentially LacY may achieve varied roles from the same amino acid sequence through an unusual flip-flopping mechanism. This fruitful “repurposing” of genetic material highlights the remarkable adaptability of living organisms and their membranes. Altering E. coli lipids disrupts growth, but controlled membrane protein flipping simulates natural selection and resemonstrates that membrane proteins can re-evolve under the selective pressure of an altered lipid bilayer.

10.1007/s11102-026-01776-5.abstract: PURPOSE: Somatotroph pituitary adenomas are a heterogeneous group comprising distinct histopathological subtypes, including the well-defined densely granulated (DG) and sparsely granulated (SG) phenotypes. While the aryl hydrocarbon receptor-interacting protein (AIP) pathway has been implicated in pituitary tumorigenesis, the role of aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator (ARNT) in somatotroph tumors remains poorly characterized. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 71 surgically treated somatotroph pituitary adenomas, clinically managed in a tertiary endocrinology center between 2020 and 2025. Immunohistochemical expression of AIP, AHR and ARNT was evaluated and correlated with clinicopathological characteristics, including cytokeratin pattern, hormonal expression and Ki-67 index. RESULTS: Moderate/strong ARNT expression was more frequent in SG than in DG adenomas (60% vs. 17.6%, p = 0.002). Patients with moderate/strong ARNT expression were younger than those with absent/weak expression (median 39 vs. 46 years, p = 0.044). In multivariable analysis, ARNT expression remained associated with the SG phenotype after adjustment for age and sex (adjusted OR 6.84, 95% CI 2.05-22.84; p = 0.002). No significant associations were observed between ARNT expression and Ki-67 index, baseline GH or IGF1 levels, AIP/AHR immunoexpression or the evaluated clinical outcomes, including biochemical control during first-generation somatostatin receptor ligand therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Increased ARNT expression is associated with the sparsely granulated phenotype in somatotroph pituitary adenomas, suggesting that ARNT expression may reflect tumor differentiation rather than proliferative activity. However, the present findings do not demonstrate additional prognostic or therapeutic utility beyond granulation pattern. Further molecular and transcriptomic studies are warranted to clarify the biological role of ARNT.

10.1002/bip.70127.title: Polyglycine Strands Within a Collagen Triple Helix
10.1002/bip.70127.abstract: ABSTRACT The collagen triple helix is the most abundant protein structural motif in animals. It tolerates any amino acid in its Xaa and Yaa positions but demands glycine (Gly) at every third position, where the residue packs into the sterically forbidding core of the triple helix and donates the recurring interstrand N–H⋯OC hydrogen bond that stitches the three strands together. (2 S )‐Proline (Pro) and (2 S ,4 R )‐4‐hydroxyproline (Hyp) are enriched far above their proteome‐wide abundance because they preorganize individual strands into the polyproline II conformation, lowering the entropic cost of folding. We asked whether the triple helix is intrinsically stable enough to form from strands that carry no such preorganization, that is, from polyglycine. To offset the conformational entropy of a Gly‐rich tract, we embedded Gly 6 within flanking triple‐helical (Pro‐Hyp‐Gly) n clamps in Ac‐(Pro‐Hyp‐Gly) 6 ‐Gly 6 ‐(Pro‐Hyp‐Gly) 5 ‐Pro‐Hyp‐NH 2 and compared it with an otherwise identical peptide in which Gly 6 was replaced by two [2‐(2‐aminoethoxy)ethoxy]acetic acid units, a flexible, length‐matched spacer that lacks most of the regularly spaced backbone amides of Gly 6 . Circular dichroism spectroscopy revealed the diagnostic positive band at 225 nm. The molar ellipticity of the spacer‐containing control was 86% of that of the Gly 6 ‐containing peptide, matching the 35/41 = 85% ratio of residues capable of triple‐helix formation and consistent with the Gly 6 segment contributing to the triple‐helical signal. Thermal denaturation yielded a T m of 46.8°C for the Gly 6 ‐containing peptide, 6.3°C higher than that of the matched spacer control. This added stability indicates that the polyglycine tract is not merely accommodated within the helix but contributes stabilizing interstrand hydrogen bonds. Together, these data indicate that three polyglycine strands can form a collagen triple helix when flanked by triple‐helical clamps. This result is consistent with the idea that the triple‐helical architecture predates the recruitment of Pro and Hyp, informs the evolutionary origin of collagen, and offers a blunt‐ended, symmetric scaffold for designing peptidic triple helices.

These results emphasize that enhancing the quality of sustainability reporting requires the integration of ethical orientations with formal governance structures. 10.54878/9bv6m266.title: Artificial Intelligence in Next-Generation Firewalls for Discriminating Cyber Attacks from Legitimate Service Traffic Surges
10.54878/9bv6m266.abstract: Next-generation firewalls (NGFWs) sit on the critical path between public networks and production services. Their most consequential error is no longer a missed signature; it is the inability to tell a malicious flood from a genuine surge in legitimate demand. Flash crowds, seasonal campaigns, media-driven spikes, and elastic microservice fan-out can resemble distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) traffic in volume while remaining economically and operationally valid. Static access-control lists, fixed rate limits, and signature catalogs therefore produce an unacceptable trade-off: either they under-block stealthy application-layer attacks or they over-block paying users. This article reviews, compares, and synthesizes peer-reviewed evidence from 2020 onward on machine-learning and deep-learning methods that can be embedded in NGFW and software-defined enforcement points to discriminate attacks from legitimate service-intensity bursts. We organize the literature into statistical filters, classical classifiers, representation-learning hybrids, sequential models, and two-tier designs that first cheaply detect a burst and then classify its intent. Published detectors regularly report accuracy above 98% on CICDDoS2019 and related traces, yet most benchmarks omit a dedicated flash-event class, which inflates apparent performance and leaves the operationally hardest decision under-tested. Building on that gap, we propose AID-NGFW, a three-tier architecture that couples entropy and cumulative-sum screening with a calibrated three-class discriminator (benign, flash crowd, attack) and a policy engine that drops malicious flows while scaling or shaping legitimate surges. Comparative tables and figures compile reported accuracies, F1-scores, datasets, and latency–accuracy trade-offs. We argue that the scientific and engineering priority is no longer binary attack detection in isolation, but reliable, low-latency, and explainable discrimination under encrypted traffic, class imbalance, concept drift, and adversarial mimicry.

10.1007/s00265-026-03810-9.abstract: Abstract African snakes display a range of defensive behaviours. However, there are limited quantifiable data on specific retaliatory behaviours for most species in response to threat-eliciting stimuli and the factors that might influence defensive behaviours, particularly in instances of human-snake conflict. We investigated defensive striking behaviour of four African snake species: puff adder ( Bitis arietans ), black mamba ( Dendroaspis polylepis ), snouted cobra ( Naja annulifera ) and Mozambique spitting cobra ( Naja mossambica ), including the impact of snake body size and sex on striking behaviours and strike performance. Individuals were presented with a fake arm model to simulate a human arm, and behaviours were recorded in two sequential trials. Of the 14 D. polylepis individuals tested, ten defensively struck at the hand and eight of these individuals bit the hand. Three of the seven N. annulifera struck with only two resulting in bites and of the six B. arietans individuals, four struck the hand and three bit the hand. None of the 21 N. mossambica individuals struck or bit the hand. Body size and sex were not significant predictors of striking behaviour. Defensive behaviours were generally higher for individuals undergoing a second trial. Strike performance results showed that B. arietans displayed the highest strike accelerations over short distances, indicating high strike effectiveness at close range. This likely contributes to its status as the species responsible for most snakebite incidences in South Africa. The results revealed that snakes exhibit a flight response when provided the opportunity to escape, but if persistently harassed, they will strike and bite in defence.

10.1186/s13100-026-00417-9.title: Quieting the HUSH: a systematic review on drug development against the human silencing hub
10.1186/s13100-026-00417-9.abstract: Abstract The Human Silencing Hub (HUSH) complex is an epigenetic regulator that maintains transcriptional repression of transposable elements and other genomic loci though deposition of the repressive histone mark H3K9 trimethylation. Composed of core scaffold proteins TASOR, MPP8, and PPHLN1, and associated effectors including SETDB1, MORC2, and ZNF638, the HUSH complex enforces epigenetic silencing that limits expression of endogenous retroelements and suppresses innate immune activation. Disruption of this pathway induces viral mimicry though accumulation of double-stransded RNA (dsRNA), activating interferon signaling, enhancing antigen presentation, and promoting antitumor immunity. Consequently, pharmacologic inhibition of HUSH components represents a promising strategy to overcome tumor immune evasion and improve response to immunotherapy. This systematic review evaluates translational efforts targeting HUSH associated proteins, analyzing 26 original research studies identified though PRISMA-guided screening. These studies investigated 23 small molecules and 3 RNA-based therapeutics across 37 cancer types, with the majority targeting the catalytic methyltransferase SETDB1. Therapeutic strategies targeting HUSH-associated silencing include FDA-approved agents, repurposed targeted therapies, novel small-molecule inhibitors, and RNA-based modalities. These therapeutic strategies disrupt epigenetic repression though mechanisms such as transcriptional modulation, interference with chromatin-binding domains, and post-transcriptional regulation of HUSH components. Collectively, these findings identify emerging pharmacologic strategies for disrupting HUSH-associated silencing, although the available evidence remains predominantly preclinical and is heavily concentrated on SETDB1. Further development and validation of selective inhibitors, including evaluation in combination with immune checkpoint blockade and radiotherapy, will be necessary to determine the therapeutic potential and clinical feasibility of targeting HUSH-associated pathways.

10.30574/ijsra.2026.21.1.1912.abstract: Ribosome collisions are increasingly invoked in infection biology, but translational arrest, physical collision, stress-kinase activation and host protection are often treated as interchangeable observations. This critical narrative review asks when translation damage is causally linked to innate-immune outcome. Targeted PubMed searches updated through 13 October 2026 prioritized primary studies with direct disome or structural evidence, pathway perturbation, genetic epistasis and infection or tissue endpoints. We distinguish pausing, stalling and physical collision, then integrate EDF1–GIGYF2–4EHP initiation control, ZNF598–ASCC/RQT and PELO–HBS1L–ABCE1 rescue, NEMF–LTN1 nascent-chain disposal, and ZAKα- and GCN2-dependent signalling. Antiviral effectors can generate stall- and collision-prone states: OAS–RNase L leaves translated cleavage products that form terminal stalls and, where ribosome density permits, collisions, whereas viperin-derived ddhCTP induces a ZAK–GCN2-dependent translational brake in defined flavivirus models. Pathogens can damage rRNA or eEF2, engineer structured pause sites, suppress ribosome influx or exploit quality-control-mediated recycling. Across these settings, collision is neither intrinsically antiviral nor synonymous with inflammation. We therefore separate causal confidence from biological relevance in a two-axis C0–C4/R0–R3 framework and use a traffic-and-threshold synthesis in which ribosome influx, lesion lifetime, rescue capacity, cell lineage and coincident pattern-recognition signals shape repair, adaptation, inflammatory alarm or cell death. Current evidence establishes collision-dependent immune signalling in only a limited set of systems; in many others, collision remains inferred from stall- or stress-associated readouts. Ribosome collision is therefore not a pathogen-specific receptor but one physical state within a broader translation-surveillance network that can couple damage to stress and innate-immune outputs.

10.1016/j.radcr.2026.09.071.abstract: Mesenteric venous thrombosis is an uncommon yet potentially life-threatening cause of mesenteric ischemia with an insidious clinical course. Delayed diagnosis of venous ischemia may lead to late complications such as bowel strictures, perforation, and fistulization. These sequelae can closely mimic Crohn's disease, posing significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. We report the case of a 33-year-old postpartum woman who presented with acute abdominal pain and was diagnosed with subacute thrombosis of the superior mesenteric vein and portal vein confluence on contrast-enhanced CT. Initial imaging demonstrated jejunal wall thickening without signs of transmural necrosis, and the patient was managed conservatively with anticoagulation. Despite treatment, she later developed recurrent abdominal pain, bowel obstruction, perforation, and complex small bowel fistulization. Serial imaging findings were initially interpreted as fibrostenotic Crohn's disease. Endoscopic evaluation and bowel biopsies were unremarkable. Ongoing recurrent obstruction ultimately necessitated limited small bowel resection, and histopathologic findings confirmed ischemic injury, characterized by ulceration, vascular congestion, granulation tissue, and full-thickness hyalinization and necrosis. The patient unfortunately died from postoperative complications seven months after the initial presentation. This case highlights chronic ischemic enteritis as an important masquerader of Crohn's disease, particularly in patients with a history of mesenteric venous thrombosis. Complex fistulization and fibrostenotic changes are not pathognomonic for inflammatory bowel disease and may represent late sequelae of missed or patchy bowel ischemia. Careful assessment of mesenteric vasculature and collateral formation on imaging is crucial to avoid misdiagnosis, inappropriate immunosuppressive therapy, and delayed definitive management.

10.1007/s12602-026-11254-w.title: Mechanistic Insights into the Antifungal Activity of the Synthetic Peptide FK18 Against Candida tropicalis
10.1007/s12602-026-11254-w.abstract: Abstract The increasing incidence of invasive fungal infections caused by opportunistic yeasts, particularly Candida tropicalis , poses a major clinical challenge due to rising antifungal resistance and the limited availability of effective therapies. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have emerged as promising alternatives owing to their rapid mechanisms of action and low propensity for resistance development. In this study, we investigated the antifungal activity, mechanism of action, and structural properties of FK18, a rationally designed synthetic cationic peptide. FK18 exhibited broad-spectrum antifungal activity against Candida and Cryptococcus species, with minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values ranging from 5 to > 40 µM. Notably, C. tropicalis showed high susceptibility, with inhibition observed at 10 µM. Time-kill assays demonstrated rapid fungicidal activity, with FK18 at 10 µM (MIC) achieving complete elimination of C. tropicalis cells within four hours. Checkerboard assays revealed strong synergistic interactions between FK18 and fluconazole, significantly reducing the concentrations required for growth inhibition. Mechanistic studies using the fluorescent probe SYTOX Green demonstrated rapid membrane permeabilization. Additionally, supplementation with exogenous ergosterol resulted in a four-fold increase in MIC, suggesting that FK18 activity is influenced by sterol-containing membranes. Nuclear magnetic resonance analyses showed that FK18 adopts a stable amphipathic α-helical structure in membrane-mimetic environments, consistent with membrane-active AMPs. Molecular dynamics simulations further supported these findings, revealing stable interactions with POPC/ergosterol lipid bilayers. Furthermore, FK18 exhibited antioxidant activity, showing significant DPPH radical scavenging activity, whereas no significant ABTS radical scavenging activity was detected up to 128 µM. Collectively, these results highlight FK18 as a multifunctional peptide with rapid fungicidal activity, membrane-targeting properties, and synergistic potential, supporting its development as a promising antifungal candidate.

10.1007/s44163-026-02602-4.normalized_title: a scoping review mapping the role of husserlian phenomenology in artificial intelligence research
10.1007/s44163-026-02602-4.title: A scoping review mapping the role of Husserlian phenomenology in artificial intelligence research
10.1007/s44163-026-02602-4.abstract: AI research increasingly attributes perception, understanding, agency, and consciousness to artificial systems. Husserlian phenomenology offers distinctions through which to examine these claims. This scoping review maps explicit Husserlian uptake in AI and robotics and asks how conceptual engagement relates to methodological and design contributions. Eight primary queries and one overlapping name-variant query were executed through the Semantic Scholar Academic Graph API on 5 December 2025. English-language publications within a 1989–2026 search window were screened for substantive AI or robotics relevance and an explicit Husserlian anchor. Of 5,594 retrieved records, 32 publications from 1990 to 2025 were included. Nine publications recovered by a post hoc PhilPapers check were charted separately using the existing codebook; they were not added to the formal corpus. The corpus clusters around embodied AI, AI epistemology, cognitive architectures, and machine consciousness, with a newer generative-AI cluster. Constitution, intentionality, horizonality, and the lifeworld recur prominently. Conceptual translation, critique, and agenda setting predominate within this sample. Methodological import or design guidance occurs in seven of the 32 publications and three of the nine external publications. That difference qualifies generalization of the quantitative balance. Across both sets, Husserlian uptake spans conceptual interpretation, methodological transfer, and architectural proposals. The synthesis shows how distinctions concerning temporality, embodiment, and evidence can structure design and evaluation questions, while separating the authors’ research proposals from the mapped findings.

10.9734/jeai/2026/v48i114592.title: Role of Cerium Oxide Nanoparticles in Improving Crop Drought Tolerance: A Review
10.9734/jeai/2026/v48i114592.abstract: Drought stress is a major constraint on crop growth and productivity because it disrupts plant water relations, photosynthesis, mineral nutrition and cellular redox balance. Cerium oxide nanoparticles (CeO₂ NPs), also known as nanoceria, have received attention as potential agents for mitigating these effects. This review examines the physicochemical properties of nanoceria, its principal application routes and the physiological, biochemical and molecular mechanisms associated with plant responses to water deficit. Surface oxygen vacancies and Ce³⁺/Ce⁴⁺ redox cycling contribute to the enzyme-mimetic activity of nanoceria and its interactions with reactive oxygen species. The reviewed studies describe responses following seed priming, foliar application and root or soil exposure. Evidence from sorghum, mungbean, barley, rice, grapevine, apple and wheat indicates that suitable nanoparticle concentrations may reduce oxidative damage, enhance antioxidant defences, protect photosynthetic functions and improve plant water status. Reported responses also include osmolyte accumulation, greater membrane stability, changes in mineral nutrient homeostasis and altered expression of drought-responsive genes. However, these outcomes depend on the crop species, nanoparticle concentration, application method and severity of water deficit. Higher concentrations may produce adverse effects, and findings from composite formulations cannot always be attributed to unmodified nanoceria. Limited field validation, incomplete understanding of root-level responses and unresolved questions about cerium accumulation in edible tissues restrict immediate agricultural application. Further evaluation is necessary to determine the consistency, practical relevance and safety of nanoceria-mediated drought responses.

10.1038/s41467-026-78942-7.title: Designing rigid protein fiducials to visualize GPCR conformational states
10.1038/s41467-026-78942-7.abstract: G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) mediate precise ligand-specific signaling profiles, yet structural visualization of how ligands alter receptor conformational landscapes in the absence of signaling partners or mimetics has proven challenging. Here we show that by combining generative protein design with deep-learning based ensemble prediction we can reliably design fiducial markers to facilitate cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) of GPCRs at arbitrary fusion points, enabling the visualization of previously intractable states. We validate the approach with high-throughput determination of inactive state structures of four pharmaceutically relevant GPCRs, allowing for key details of receptor pharmacology to be resolved in each case. We then engineered an extracellular fiducial marker for the prototypical β2-adrenergic receptor that enabled direct structural characterization of the rearrangement of key intracellular motifs in the absence of G-protein. Comparison with recent co-folding models highlights major gaps in current methods for predicting ligand-induced GPCR conformations. These results present a generalizable framework for accessing traditionally inaccessible structural states of small, dynamic proteins. Visualizing how drugs reshape GPCR receptors by cryo-EM has been difficult for many conformational states. Here, authors use designed protein fiducials to image elusive GPCR states, revealing details of ligand induced receptor activation.

10.1186/s12887-026-07764-9.normalized_title: severe functional constipation masquerading as acute intracranial infection in an adolescent a diagnostic pitfall and the risks of empirical mannitol therapy a case report
10.1186/s12887-026-07764-9.title: Severe functional constipation masquerading as acute intracranial infection in an adolescent: a diagnostic pitfall and the risks of empirical mannitol therapy — a case report
10.1186/s12887-026-07764-9.abstract: Abstract Background The differential diagnosis and treatment of non-specific neurological manifestations in adolescents (such as headaches and impaired consciousness) remain a significant challenge in clinical practice. Current clinical routine tends to prioritize the investigation of infectious etiologies, yet functional gastrointestinal disorders are frequently overlooked during screening. Furthermore, in cases of suspected increased intracranial pressure, empirical treatment is often initiated without objective measurement of intracranial pressure, which carries underappreciated risks. Case presentation We report a case of a 14-year-old female patient presenting with sudden bilateral temporal headache, dizziness, and a 21-hour episode of stupor that had spontaneously resolved before hospital arrival. On admission she was alert but lethargic, with normal vital signs, normal neurological examination, and an unremarkable head CT. She was empirically treated with acyclovir and intravenous mannitol for suspected intracranial infection with presumed elevated intracranial pressure. However, subsequent investigations did not support either diagnosis: cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal with an opening pressure of 70 mmH 2 O (below the pediatric reference range, measured after mannitol administration), fundoscopic examination revealed no papilledema, and brain MRI showed no infectious or structural abnormalities. Persistent headache and lethargy continued despite mannitol therapy. During hospitalization, the patient developed severe constipation. An upright abdominal radiograph demonstrated extensive fecal retention and gaseous distension throughout the colon, together with an incidental finding of non-fusion of the posterior vertebral arches at S1–S2. Following bowel evacuation and discontinuation of mannitol, the persistent headache and lethargy substantially improved, with no recurrence during 3-month follow-up. Conclusions This case illustrates that empirical osmotherapy for presumed intracranial hypertension, in the absence of objective evidence from relevant examinations—such as cerebrospinal fluid pressure measurements—may be both ineffective and potentially harmful. Clinicians should base decisions about osmotherapy on objective intracranial pressure assessment rather than presumptive diagnosis, and should include gastrointestinal evaluation in the work-up of adolescents with persistent unexplained neurological symptoms. Incidental anatomical findings such as isolated posterior arch defects should not be over-interpreted in the absence of dedicated MRI evaluation.

10.1016/j.jot.2026.101244.title: Macrophage reprogramming in degenerative musculoskeletal diseases: From tissue-niche biology to therapeutic translation
10.1016/j.jot.2026.101244.abstract: Degenerative musculoskeletal diseases (DMSDs), including osteoarthritis (OA), osteoporosis (OP), intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD), and sarcopenia (SP), impose a major burden through pain, structural deterioration, mobility loss, fracture risk, and functional decline. Although these disorders are often grouped as age-related musculoskeletal conditions, they arise from distinct tissue niches and cannot be explained by a single pathogenic mechanism. Macrophages occupy a central position at the interface between degenerative stress and tissue outcome, but their functions extend far beyond a binary M1/M2 polarization model. This Review proposes a disease-niche-adapted framework for macrophage reprogramming in DMSDs. In this framework, macrophages are interpreted according to the pathological tasks they perform within each tissue environment: inflammatory amplification and pain-related synovial crosstalk in OA, osteoimmune remodeling in OP, immune-barrier disruption and macrophage-nucleus pulposus (NP) cell feedback in IVDD, and impaired regenerative support in aging muscle in SP. We discuss how macrophage functional states are shaped by transcriptional and epigenetic regulation, immunometabolic rewiring, inflammatory signaling, autophagy and organelle quality control, and local niche-derived cues. Therapeutic strategies are then evaluated according to whether they interrupt upstream niche stress, redirect inflammatory and metabolic decoding, restore quality-control capacity, or reshape macrophage-mediated tissue communication. Finally, we propose that macrophage-targeted therapy should be assessed through a hierarchy of evidence, progressing from marker changes to functional reprogramming, macrophage-causal validation, and disease-specific structural or functional improvement. This framework may help convert macrophage plasticity from a broad immunological concept into a more precise, testable, and disease-adapted therapeutic strategy for musculoskeletal degeneration. The translational potential of this article This Review provides a disease-niche-adapted framework for evaluating macrophage reprogramming in degenerative musculoskeletal diseases. By linking disease-specific macrophage tasks with regulatory mechanisms, therapeutic entry points, causal validation, delivery feasibility, and tissue-relevant endpoints, this framework may help guide both the design and translational assessment of macrophage-targeted interventions for musculoskeletal degeneration.

10.24093/awejtls/vol10no4.11.title: Hollow Identity: A Comparative Study of Identity Formation and Resistance in Adichie’s Americanah and Mbue’s Behold the Dreamers
10.24093/awejtls/vol10no4.11.abstract: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s Americanah (2013) and Imbolo Mbue’s Behold the Dreamers (2016) focus on the challenges African immigrants face in finding their identity and acceptance in a foreign society. Therefore, this study aims to illustrate how migration reshapes identity and how African immigrants seek belonging while using different forms of resistance in both novels. The study’s significance lies in the examination of how migration can change identity and how African immigrants use subtle resistance to cope with the challenges of belonging and displacement. By introducing the concept of “hollow identity,” in which African immigrants are physically present in the host country but emotionally disconnected from their homeland, the study shows how this condition leads them to use unique forms of resistance. Through postcolonial theory, especially Homi K. Bhabha’s notions of hybridity and mimicry, Stuart Hall’s views about identity in terms of “being” and “becoming”, and James C. Scott’s theory of everyday resistance, the research focuses on the process of identity formation via displacement and race. The analysis concludes that returning home does not restore immigrants’ original identities; instead, it reveals that migration leaves them feeling detached from their cultural roots. It also demonstrates that the characters’ identities are unstable, so their resistance often takes subtle forms, expressed through everyday actions rather than direct confrontation.

10.1002/ccr3.73677.title: Villoglandular Adenocarcinoma of the Cervix With Ovarian Metastasis Mimicking a Borderline Ovarian Tumor: A Rare Case Report
10.1002/ccr3.73677.abstract: ABSTRACT This case reports rare cervical villoglandular adenocarcinoma metastasizing to the ovary with a deceptive borderline‐like morphology. Diagnosis relied on matching immunohistochemistry and HPV16 DNA detection in both sites. The patient underwent surgery and chemoradiotherapy, remaining recurrence‐free. This highlights the critical need for multimodal testing to distinguish such metastases from primary ovarian tumors.
